grades.quote: For example, a page can be marked as readable, writable, and executable when in kernel mode, but totally inaccessible when in user mode. In this case, the page table need not be changed when switching operating modes. If the kernel uses the same page table as the user-mode process, then the range of addresses occupied by the kernel will be off limits to the process. The IA-32 architecture fits this pattern.
grades.reason: Directly answers the query. Each page table entry holds separate protection settings for kernel and user mode. Kernel pages are marked inaccessible in user mode, so the kernel's address range is off limits to user processes even with a shared page table. The passage names IA-32 as an example and gives the Linux 3 GiB user / 1 GiB kernel split.
Covers protection keys on Itanium in single-address-space systems. It does not cover IA-32 or user/kernel separation through mode-specific page table protections.
